## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways based on a combination of statistical significance, biological coherence, and relevance to stroke pathophysiology. Notably, immune and inflammatory pathways are strongly represented, including antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via major histocompatibility complex class one (Gene Ontology:0002474, p = 3.38 × 10−3), Interleukin ten signaling (Reactome:R-HSA-6783783, p = 9.39 × 10−5), cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, p = 5.32 × 10−16), tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (Reactome:R-HSA-5669034, p = 5.55 × 10−10), and regulation of leukocyte activation (Gene Ontology:0002694, p = 1.03 × 10−8). These findings are highly consistent with the established literature showing that stroke triggers rapid activation of innate and adaptive immune responses, cytokine release, antigen presentation, and leukocyte recruitment, all of which contribute to secondary brain injury and post-stroke inflammation.  

Furthermore, pathways related to extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue barrier disruption are also prominent, including extracellular matrix structural constituent (Gene Ontology:0005201, p = 3.81 × 10−8), external encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p = 9.27 × 10−17), matrix metalloproteinases (WikiPathways:129, p = 4.38 × 10−3), and endopeptidase inhibitor activity (Gene Ontology:0004866, p = 5.57 × 10−4). This pattern is biologically relevant because extracellular matrix degradation and protease imbalance are well-known drivers of blood-brain barrier breakdown, edema, and hemorrhagic transformation after stroke; matrix metalloproteinases in particular have been repeatedly implicated in ischemic brain injury in experimental and clinical studies. In addition, enrichment of mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04010, p = 3.67 × 10−4) supports the involvement of stress-response signaling cascades that regulate inflammation, apoptosis, and neuronal survival after cerebral ischemia.  

Additional signals, such as the HRD1 complex (Comprehensive Resource of Mammalian Protein Complexes:6859, p = 3.09 × 10−2) and receptor complex (Gene Ontology:0043235, p = 2.58 × 10−7), may reflect altered protein quality control and receptor-mediated signaling during ischemic stress. Although tissue-enrichment terms involving appendix goblet cells and colon goblet cells from the Human Protein Atlas likely reflect expression overlap rather than stroke-specific mechanisms, the overall pathway landscape strongly supports a model in which stroke is characterized by coordinated inflammatory activation, cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix injury, and stress-response pathway engagement, with the very small p-values across several terms providing strong statistical support for these shared mechanisms.
